blocking.issue: New regression from the revision. The throttle now has max(1, GOMAXPROCS/4) hash slots, a success cache that hits do not extend, and a full cache flush on every snapshot swap and revocation advance. Together these put an unstated ceiling on legitimate `auth.basic` traffic and cause a 429 storm after every configuration change. An operator cannot tell from the document whether `auth.basic` fits their workload. On a 4-core Node there is 1 slot, which verifies 10 to 20 credentials per second (hypothesis). Every active client must be re-verified every 60 s, so the Node sustains only about 600 to 1,200 distinct active credentials, while the success cache is sized for 10,000. After each Hot Reload or Rollout, or after any revocation entry (for example a JWT `jti` logout unrelated to basic auth), every cached client misses at once. Only 1 slot plus 4 waiters are admitted within the 1 s deadline, so nearly all other legitimate callers get 429 RZ-AUTH-007. Neither the capacity bound nor the flush storm appears in the residuals or in OQ-security-and-identity-15.
blocking.evidence: Line 402: "Success cache | HMAC-SHA-256 under a per-process key; 60 s from verification, not extended by hits; 64 shards, 10,000 entries per Node (target); flushed on each snapshot swap and revocation advance". Line 404: "Hash queue | max(1, `GOMAXPROCS`/4) slots, which cap the Node's hash rate; 4 × slots waiters, 1 s deadline (target); overflow gets RZ-AUTH-007 unhashed". Line 409: "At 600,000 iterations a slot verifies 10 to 20 credentials per second (hypothesis)".
blocking.fix: (1) State the capacity: "a Node sustains about slots x 10 to 20 x 60 distinct active `auth.basic` credentials (hypothesis); `auth.basic` suits low-cardinality clients, and high-cardinality callers SHOULD use API keys or JWT". (2) Stop flushing the whole cache. On a snapshot swap, keep entries whose Consumer credential digest is unchanged in the new snapshot, and on a revocation advance evict only entries for the revoked usernames or digests. Or spread re-verification over time and state the resulting 429 bound (target). (3) Size the success cache to the sustainable rate, or state why 10,000 is correct. (4) Add the capacity bound and the flush behavior to the T1 residuals and to OQ-security-and-identity-15.

blocking.section: Request hardening (Pre-authentication throttling, 'Unknown usernames' and 'Username bucket' rows)
blocking.issue: The new unknown-username rule claims that "timing reveals nothing", but the design lets an attacker enumerate usernames through the throttle state. All unknown usernames share one bucket, while each known username gets its own bucket with a burst of 10. An attacker first empties the shared bucket with a few junk usernames, then probes a candidate. An unknown candidate is delayed up to 2 s or refused with 429 RZ-AUTH-007. A known candidate still has a full bucket, so it is hashed and gets a 401. The status and latency differ, so a security engineer relying on the stated property is misled. The document also leaves undefined what happens to a known-username attempt once bucket creation hits its limit of 100 per second per Node (target): whether it is refused, shares a bucket, or gets no bucket.
blocking.evidence: Line 403: "Unknown usernames | One shared bucket and a dummy hash through the same queue, so timing reveals nothing". Line 405: "Username bucket | Burst 10, refill 1 per second, 64-shard LRU of 100,000 (target); created only after the hash queue admits an attempt, at most 100 per second per Node (target)".
blocking.fix: Either give each unknown username its own bucket in the same LRU, created under the same admission rule and creation cap as known ones, so throttle behavior does not depend on whether the username exists. Or keep the shared bucket, delete "so timing reveals nothing", and list username enumeration through throttle state as a T1 residual in OQ-security-and-identity-15. In both cases, state the outcome for an attempt that exceeds the bucket-creation cap, for example "429 RZ-AUTH-007 unhashed, counted by cause", and apply it to known and unknown usernames alike.
